content: Open fractures of the extremities are often complicated by wound and bone infections, which can significantly increase the associated morbidity. In developed countries, the administration of antibiotics is a standard practice as part of a comprehensive treatment protocol. This protocol typically includes wound irrigation, surgical debridement, and stabilization of the fracture when necessary. Antibiotics are believed to play a role in reducing the incidence of infections in these cases. The objective of this review was to evaluate the evidence supporting the effectiveness of antibiotics in the initial management of open limb fractures. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and International Pharmaceutical Abstracts, covering studies published up to July 2009. Additionally, proceedings from major orthopedic organizations and reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed. Researchers in the field were also contacted for further information. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving individuals of any age with open limb fractures. The intervention of interest was the administration of antibiotics either before or at the time of primary treatment, compared to placebo or no antibiotics. The outcomes assessed included early wound infection, chronic drainage, acute or chronic osteomyelitis, delayed or non-union of fractures, amputations, and mortality. Two independent reviewers screened the studies for inclusion, assessed their quality using an eight-item scale, and extracted relevant data. Additional information was obtained from three trial authors. Data from 1106 participants across eight studies were analyzed. The results demonstrated that the use of antibiotics significantly reduced the risk of early infections compared to placebo or no antibiotics. The calculated risk ratio was 0.43 (95% confidence interval: 0.29 to 0.65), with an absolute risk reduction of 7% (95% confidence interval: 3% to 10%). However, there was insufficient data to assess other outcomes such as chronic osteomyelitis, delayed unions, or amputations. The authors concluded that antibiotics are effective in reducing the incidence of early infections in open limb fractures. In middleand high-income countries, further placebo-controlled randomized trials on this topic are unlikely to be ethically justified, except potentially for open fractures of the fingers. However, additional research is needed to understand the preventable burden of morbidity in settings where antibiotics are not routinely used in the management of open fractures.
